primitives.summary: Configures the SDK for one consumer/provider pair — the object every other primitive hangs off.

signature.name: consumer
signature.description: The consumer's name, as 'consumer-session/create' records it.

signature.name: provider
signature.description: The provider's name.

signature.name: options
signature.description: Where the contract is written (default: a 'contracts' directory under the working directory), how the engine is reached (the embedding, spec.md §2; ADR 0023), how much the engine logs (below), and the project's declared components (design 2.6 §10.2) — a list of component declarations, none by default.

primitives.semantics: Makes no protocol call when constructed. The engine is started, and 'engine/hello' sent offering protocol version 1 (engine-protocol spec §5), when the first 'execute' needs it; one engine and at most one open consumer session belong to one configured object, and a test suite uses one configured object. A hello that fails, or agrees any protocol version other than 1, fails that first 'execute' with the engine's error; nothing is retried. When the options declare components, 'consumer-session/create' carries them as 'config.components', each declaration as written except that a 'file' source's 'reference' with no root is resolved against the working directory — the SDK is the loader here (lifecycle-hooks spec §7.1), and the engine resolves no path against a directory of its own. A reference has a root when it begins with a path separator or, on Windows, with a drive letter, a colon and a separator, or with a share; a reference with a root is passed as written. That includes a reference on Windows that begins with a separator and names no drive: the platform's path libraries disagree about whether that is absolute, so the rule is stated on the text and not on a library's answer. No declaration is checked, fetched or opened by the SDK: whether a component loads is the engine's answer, and a component that cannot be loaded fails the first 'execute' with the engine's 'component-unavailable'. With no components declared, 'config' carries no 'components' member. How much the engine logs is set where the language's tests set any logging, and the engine's events are shown where the language shows any log (ADR 0061): an SDK reads the language's own logging option or configuration, and passes it to the engine as 'RUST_LOG'; a 'RUST_LOG' the environment already has is passed as it is, directives included. Where the language has a logging framework to forward to, the SDK starts the engine with 'JANUS_LOG_FORMAT=json' and logs each event it writes at its own level, reading its members and never its text. How each language spells this is its style guide's.

errors.surfaced-as: thrown from the first 'execute', carrying the engine's 'details.supported' verbatim

primitives.summary: Begins a new interaction specification.
primitives.semantics: Opens a new interaction-spec document (contract spec §1, schema contract.schema.json#/$defs/InteractionSpec) with 'description' set and 'transport' set to { kind: 'http', mode: 'passive' } — 'request' and 'response' describe an HTTP exchange the consumer initiates, which is exactly a passive HTTP interaction (engine-protocol spec §8.2). No protocol call happens; the document is submitted by 'execute'. The builder is opaque to the protocol and exists only in the idiomatic layer; building the same chain twice produces two equal documents.

primitives.summary: Declares a provider state this interaction requires.

signature.name: params
signature.description: Optional state parameters, a JSON object. A member whose value is a 'when-variant' or 'variant-cases' helper is variant-bound (variant semantics spec §6); every other member is literal.

primitives.semantics: Appends { name, params, variant-params } to the interaction-spec document's 'states' array, in call order. A member of 'params' whose value is a 'when-variant' or 'variant-cases' helper is not a literal parameter: it is written instead as one binding in the entry's 'variant-params' (variant semantics spec §6.2), with 'name' set to that member's name, in the order the members were written. Every other member stays in 'params', passed through as written — no key is renamed, reordered or coerced. 'params' is omitted from the entry when it has no literal members, and 'variant-params' when it has no bindings; neither is ever written as null, {} or []. A binding helper anywhere other than as a params member's own value — inside a list, or inside a nested object — is refused at the call, because it would otherwise be written as a literal that only looks like a binding, the in-band ambiguity variant semantics spec §6.2 exists to prevent. Calling 'given' again appends a further state. The binding's dimension reference is passed through as written: resolving it against the variant space, and rejecting a reference that matches no dimension or several, or a point the dimension lacks, is the engine's (variant semantics spec §6.3, §6.5), because only the engine computes the space. Contributes nothing to the variant space.

errors.surfaced-as: thrown from 'execute' (this primitive makes no call), with the engine's 'problems' carried verbatim — e.g. a dimension reference that resolves to nothing, pointed at '/states/<i>/variant-params/<j>/dimension'

primitives.summary: A provider-state parameter that is true exactly when the running variant is at one point of one dimension — the RFC's 'whenVariant'.

signature.name: dimension
signature.description: A dimension reference: its full id, its full path, or a trailing run of whole path segments ('shippedAt', 'response.body.shippedAt#presence').

signature.name: point
signature.description: One of that dimension's point names ('present', 'SHIPPED', 'min+1').

primitives.semantics: Valid only as the value of a 'given' params member, which names the parameter. Written as the binding { name, dimension, cases: [ { point, value: true } ], default: false } — ADR 0009's two-case boolean form, spelled with a 'default' rather than a second case so that it means the same thing for a dimension of any number of points, and for a gated dimension, which variant semantics spec §6.5 requires to have a 'default'. 'dimension' and 'point' are written as given.

primitives.summary: A provider-state parameter whose value is chosen by the running variant's point for one dimension.

signature.name: dimension
signature.description: A dimension reference, as for 'when-variant'.

signature.name: cases
signature.description: Point name -> the parameter's value at that point. At least one.

signature.name: default
signature.description: Optional: the value when the dimension is inactive or at a point no case names.

primitives.semantics: Valid only as the value of a 'given' params member, which names the parameter. Written as the binding { name, dimension, cases, default } of variant semantics spec §6.2: 'cases' as a list of { point, value }, one per member of the map, in the order the members were written; 'default' omitted when not given — never written as null, since null is a value a parameter can take. With no default, a variant at a point no case names leaves the parameter absent (variant semantics spec §6.4). An empty map is refused at the call, since a binding with no case can only ever be its default.

primitives.summary: Declares the request part of an HTTP interaction.

signature.name: parts
signature.description: Any of method, path, query, headers and body.

primitives.semantics: Populates 'parts.request', one slot per member given; a member not given produces no slot. 'method', 'path' and 'body' are compiled by the 'literal' rules (this document) — a bare value becomes an 'equality' node, a shape helper is used as authored — and are otherwise untouched: the method is not upper-cased and the path is not normalised, because repairing a value is the engine's call to reject, not the SDK's to make (SDK spec §2.1). 'query' and 'headers' are each a map of name to value and compile to an 'object' node with one member per name, because the HTTP transport carries each as a map of name to a list of values (shape spec §3.6): a string value becomes an 'equality' node over the one-element list [value]; a list becomes an 'equality' node over that list, each element written by the same rule; a shape helper describes the one value and becomes an 'each-like' node whose 'items' is that shape, with 'min' 1 and 'max' 1 — exactly one value, matching it. A helper whose node admits absence is the exception, because absence is a fact about the member and not about the value in it: the list treatment applies inside the modifier, never to it. So 'forbidden' becomes the member's shape directly — there is nothing to carry a list — and 'optional(of)' becomes an 'optional' node whose 'of' is the 'each-like' the rule would otherwise have built, leaving the presence dimension on the header or query name itself (shape spec §6.4), where an author who wrote 'this header may be absent' means it to be. Wrapping instead of excepting would put a node admitting absence in an 'each-like's 'items', which shape spec §5.1 refuses, so the natural spelling would build a document the engine rejects while the document it meant would have no spelling at all. The bounds are written because an unbounded 'each-like' contributes a cardinality dimension (shape spec §6.4), which on the request side would require the consumer to send the header twice in some variant; bounded at one, the dimension has a single point and contributes nothing. Several values each matching a shape are not expressible through this rule. A value that is not a string is written as the one string that spells it, but only where every language spells it the same way: a whole number whose magnitude is at most 2^53 - 1 becomes its shortest decimal form (no exponent, no trailing zeros, no leading '+', so 3 and 3.0 are the same value and both are written '3'), and a boolean becomes 'true' or 'false'. Every other value is refused at the call, before any document is built — a number with a fractional part or a larger magnitude, a date or a time, null, a map, a list holding any of these — because a value whose spelling differs by language ('1.5e3' or '1500.0'; '1e+21' or '1.0E21') would make two SDKs send different bytes for the same test, and a date has no format the SDK may choose (compare 'datetime', this document). This is not the coercion 'method' and 'path' forbid: those are values the engine judges as the author wrote them, while a header or query value reaches the transport as a string and nothing else (shape spec §3.6), which is why this rule already writes a bare string as a one-element list. Header names are lower-cased, which is the only spelling the HTTP transport presents them under, since HTTP header names are case-insensitive; query names are kept exactly as written, since they are not. Two header names that are the same once lower-cased are refused at the call, for the reason 'regex' refuses a flag it cannot carry (this document): the SDK made the collision by lower-casing, the engine never sees the declaration that would be dropped, and an author who means one header with two values writes the list form.

errors.surfaced-as: thrown from 'execute' (this primitive makes no call), with the engine's 'problems' — each a 'pointer' into the interaction-spec document and a 'message' — carried verbatim

primitives.summary: Declares the response part of an HTTP interaction.

signature.name: parts
signature.description: Any of status, headers and body.

primitives.semantics: Identical treatment to 'request' (this document), populating 'parts.response': 'status' and 'body' by the 'literal' rules, 'headers' by the name-to-list rule with names lower-cased.

primitives.summary: Submits an interaction and runs the test closure once per variant the engine selects.

signature.name: interaction
signature.description: A built interaction ('interaction' and its chain).

signature.name: closure
signature.description: Runs once per selected variant, receiving (mock, variant).

primitives.semantics: In order: 'create' with the configured consumer and provider, if this configured object has no open session yet (one session per suite — sessions amortise state and transport setup, and 'finalise' writes all of a suite's interactions into one contract); 'add-interaction' with the built document; 'start-transport' with transport 'http', if the session has not started one; 'variants' for the returned handle. Then, for each variant in the order 'variants' returned them: 'serve-variant' with that variant's 'id', then the closure with (mock, variant) — 'mock' exposes the transport's 'endpoint' descriptor and, for HTTP, its 'base-url' as 'mock.url'; 'variant' is the descriptor exactly as 'variants' returned it (id and label — variant semantics spec §2.2; assignment and origin — §3.9). The closure runs once per selected variant, never once per declared variant, and never zero times: a one-variant selection still runs it once. A closure that throws or rejects fails that variant only: every remaining variant still runs, and 'execute' then fails once, naming every failed variant by label and id with its cause. An engine error is not a closure's verdict and is not recorded as one: when any operation 'execute' sends answers with an error — including a 'serve-variant' inside the loop — 'execute' fails at once with that error, and the variants after it do not run. The guarantee above is about what a test decided; an engine that cannot arm this variant cannot arm the next one either, and one failure per remaining variant would say the tests failed when the engine did. 'execute' does not decide whether any variant passed from the values the mock saw — the engine's verdict on each exchange (a request that did not match, a variant never exercised) is returned by 'finalise', and 'finalise' fails on it (this document).

errors.surfaced-as: thrown before any variant runs, from 'add-interaction', 'problems' verbatim
thrown before any variant runs, from 'variants'
thrown from 'execute', like any engine error (this document). The SDK owns the session's lifetime end to end, so reaching a user means the engine lost the session — never something the caller did

primitives.summary: Ends the suite's session, and writes the contract if the engine produced one.
primitives.semantics: Sends 'finalise' for the open session, if there is one, and then ends the engine (engine-protocol spec §6 — for the subprocess embedding, closing its stdin). When the result carries 'contract' — present iff every interaction verified on every variant it required (engine-protocol spec §8.2) — writes it to '<contract directory>/<consumer>-<provider>.janus.json' (the '.janus.json' suffix is contract spec §2.3's convention; the '<consumer>-<provider>' stem is this primitive's) as compact UTF-8 JSON followed by one LF (contract spec §2.4), members in the order the engine returned them; the SDK never reorders, merges or edits a contract. When it does not, fails, naming every interaction and variant whose status is not 'verified' with the engine's mismatches, and writes nothing. It also writes nothing, and fails naming the interactions, when any 'execute' in the session failed — even though the engine returned a contract: the engine verified the exchanges, but only the closure knows whether the consumer handled what it was sent, and a contract must not claim a variant the consumer's own test failed on. (The protocol cannot yet tell the engine that a closure failed; until it can, this is the one verdict the SDK holds that the engine does not.) The test-framework integration MUST run 'finalise' after the suite's last 'execute', including when an 'execute' failed: sessions are the only resource (engine-protocol spec §7.1) and 'finalise' is the only way to release one. Calling it with no open session ends the engine and does nothing else.

primitives.summary: A plain value where a shape is expected — no helper call at all.
primitives.semantics: The rule every other primitive's 'nested-shape' parameter, and every member of a request or response part, is compiled by. A shape helper's result is used as authored. A string, number, boolean or null becomes an 'equality' node with the value as its example (shape spec §4.1). An object — a plain map written in the DSL, not a helper's result — becomes an 'object' node with one member per key, each compiled by this rule, in the order written (shape-language example order-payload.md §2); members the provider sends beyond these are admitted (shape spec §4.3). A list becomes an 'array' node with one positional entry per element, each compiled by this rule (shape spec §4.1). Nothing else is inferred: no value becomes a kind predicate, a regex or an optional without its helper. How the idiomatic layer tells a helper's result from a plain map that happens to have a 'shape' member is the style guide's business; it MUST NOT be by looking for a 'shape' member.

primitives.summary: Marks a body as a JSON document.
primitives.semantics: Compiles 'document' by the 'literal' rules and adds nothing: a structured body with no declared content type is produced as application/json (contract spec §5.5, ADR 0020 decision 3), so there is nothing for 'json' to declare and no node for it to emit. It exists because the RFC's DSL names the body's content type at the call site; a body written without it compiles identically, and a body of any other type is written with 'content'.

primitives.summary: Marks a body as content of a named media type — CSV, XML, anything a declared component handles.

signature.name: media-type
signature.description: The body's media type, e.g. 'text/csv'. Written as given.

signature.name: document
signature.description: The body's shape, over the document the content component decodes the octets to.

primitives.semantics: Accepted only as the 'body' of 'request' or 'response'. There, 'document' is compiled by the 'literal' rules as that slot's shape, exactly as if it had been written without 'content', and the interaction-spec document gains 'content-types' with the media type under the part and slot — { 'response': { 'body': 'text/csv' } } (contract spec §5.5, ADR 0020). The media type is written as given: not lower-cased, not parsed, not checked against any list, because which types exist is the engine's and its components' answer, and an interaction declaring a type no loaded component handles is refused by 'add-interaction' with 'component-unavailable'. 'content' anywhere else — nested in a template, as a header or query value, as a method, path or status — is refused at the call (ADR 0019): a declaration names a whole slot, and there is no slot for it to name there. 'content' contributes no variant dimension of its own; 'document' contributes whatever its shape does.

errors.surfaced-as: thrown from 'execute', naming 'content/<media type>' as the engine does

primitives.summary: A whole-number value.
primitives.semantics: Compiles to an 'integer' kind predicate (shape spec §4.2) with 'example' as its example. Contributes no variant dimension.

primitives.summary: Any numeric value.
primitives.semantics: Compiles to a 'number' kind predicate (shape spec §4.2) with 'example' as its example. Contributes no variant dimension.

primitives.summary: A number written with a fractional part.
primitives.semantics: Compiles to a 'decimal' kind predicate (shape spec §4.2) with 'example' as its example. Where a content component cannot distinguish lexical forms this degrades to 'number' at the component boundary; the SDK still emits 'decimal'. Contributes no variant dimension.

primitives.summary: A string value.
primitives.semantics: Compiles to a 'string' kind predicate (shape spec §4.2) with 'example' as its example. Contributes no variant dimension.

primitives.summary: A boolean value.
primitives.semantics: Compiles to a 'boolean' kind predicate (shape spec §4.2) with 'example' as its example. Contributes no variant dimension.

primitives.summary: A string parsing as a datetime.

signature.name: format
signature.description: Optional, in shape spec §4.2's pattern language.

primitives.semantics: Compiles to a 'datetime' node (shape spec §4.2) with 'example' as its example and 'format' when given. When 'format' is not given the node has none — which means ISO-8601 (shape spec §4.2) — and the SDK does not infer one from the example.

primitives.summary: A string parsing as a calendar date.
primitives.semantics: Identical treatment to 'datetime' (this document), for the 'date' operator.

primitives.summary: A string parsing as a time of day.
primitives.semantics: Identical treatment to 'datetime' (this document), for the 'time' operator.

primitives.summary: A string matching a pattern.

signature.name: pattern
signature.description: RE2-compatible subset (shape spec §4.2).

primitives.semantics: Compiles to a 'regex' node with 'pattern' and 'example'. Matching is unanchored (shape spec §4.2), so the SDK MUST NOT anchor the pattern; an author who means a full match writes '^...$'. A pattern the language represents with out-of-band options — flags, modifiers — that the pattern text cannot carry is refused at the call, before any document is built: silently dropping an option would change what the pattern means.

primitives.summary: Enumerates the literal values a field may take.
primitives.semantics: Compiles to an 'any-of' node (shape spec §4.1, §5.3) with 'options' as its literal set, in the order given, and the first option as its example. Contributes one 'value' variant dimension, one point per option (shape spec §6.4) — computed by the engine, not the SDK.

primitives.summary: A discriminated union of alternatives.

signature.name: alternatives
signature.description: Name -> the alternative, a plain map binding 'discriminator' to a literal.

primitives.semantics: Compiles to a 'one-of' node with 'discriminator' and one alternative per name, in the order given, each compiled by the 'literal' rules — so the discriminator's literal becomes an 'equality' node like any other scalar. Adds no 'default': absent, the engine takes the lexicographically first alternative (shape spec §6.1). The SDK does not check that the alternatives bind distinct discriminator literals, or bind one at all: the engine rejects both with 'interaction-invalid' when the interaction is added (shape spec §5.4), and a second check here could only disagree with it. Contributes one 'alternative' variant dimension (shape spec §6.4).

errors.surfaced-as: thrown from 'execute', naming the duplicate or missing discriminator in the engine's own words

primitives.summary: Marks a value as may-be-absent.
primitives.semantics: Compiles to an 'optional' node (shape spec §4.4) wrapping 'of' compiled by the 'literal' rules, with no further transformation. Contributes one 'presence' variant dimension (shape spec §6.4).

primitives.summary: Marks a value as may-be-null.
primitives.semantics: Identical treatment to 'optional' (this document), for the 'nullable' operator (shape spec §4.4).

primitives.summary: Asserts that a member is absent.
primitives.semantics: Compiles to a 'forbidden' node (shape spec §4.4), which admits absence and nothing else. It takes no nested shape and no example — a constraint on a value that must not exist is not a thing to write — so the helper takes no arguments. Contributes no variant dimension: what it admits has one point, and only width earns a dimension (shape spec §6.1). The SDK does not check where it was written: a 'forbidden' node belongs in a slot and MUST NOT be wrapped by 'optional' or 'nullable' (shape spec §5.1, §5.2), and the engine rejects a misplaced one with 'interaction-invalid' when the interaction is added.

errors.surfaced-as: thrown from 'execute', naming the misplaced node in the engine's own words

primitives.summary: An array of like elements, with a cardinality.

signature.name: options
signature.description: Optional { min, max }.

primitives.semantics: Compiles to an 'each-like' node (shape spec §4.1) with 'items' compiled by the 'literal' rules, and 'min' and 'max' only when given — absent, 'min' means 1 and 'max' unbounded in the shape itself, so the SDK does not write the defaults. Contributes one 'cardinality' variant dimension (shape spec §6.4).

primitives.summary: Configures one provider verification: where the provider is, which pacts or contracts, and the run's options.

signature.name: options
signature.description: The provider URL (required); exactly one source: 'pacts', the paths of Janus contracts or v1–v4 pacts to read, 'broker', a broker source, or 'urls', a urls source, each as engine-protocol spec §8.3 spells it without its 'kind'; the run's 'options', as 'verification/verify' spells them (publish, filter, variants, stop-on-first-failure); 'transport', the HTTP transport's drive options beside 'base-url' (headers, client; component-interfaces spec §5.6), passed as given (ADR 0056 decision 2); 'config', the path of a project configuration file (lifecycle-hooks spec §6.1); the project's declared 'components'; and how the engine is reached, and how much it logs, as for 'janus'.

primitives.semantics: Makes no protocol call and starts no engine when constructed, and neither does declaring a handler on it ('state-handler', 'request-filter'): everything happens in 'verify' (ADR 0055 decision 1). Options naming no source, or more than one of 'pacts', 'broker' and 'urls', are refused at the call that would send them, before an engine is started, with no frame sent. Nothing in the options is checked beyond that: whether a source, a filter or a component is acceptable is the engine's answer, at 'verify'. The SDK reads no environment variable for any option, a broker's credentials included: the test passes what it wants sent.

facade.reason: the HTTP transport's 'headers' and 'client.tls.insecure' in 'transport', as S1.13 maps the CLI's --header and --disable-ssl-verification (ADR 0056 decision 2).

they ran on the edge of today's state-change calls, before an interaction's first state; a hook has no point before 'state-setup' to run them at, so the facade refuses them by name (ADR 0056 decision 4).

a state-change URL or a message transport is a hook in verifier.janus.yaml ('config'), written as janus verify writes its own (ADR 0053); the facade refuses them by name rather than writing configuration of its own (ADR 0056 decision 4).

facade.from: pact-js Verifier options (providerBaseUrl, pactUrls, pactBrokerUrl, consumerVersionSelectors, enablePending, publishVerificationResult, providerVersion)
facade.reason: each is a member of the protocol's own source or options document, spelled as the protocol spells it; the default supplied is that nothing is read from the environment, where today's verifier reads PACT_BROKER_* variables — a test reads its own and passes them (ADR 0055 decision 1).

primitives.summary: Puts the provider in a provider state before an exchange, and optionally takes it out after, in the test's own code.

signature.name: state
signature.description: The provider state's name, exactly as the pact or contract records it.

signature.name: setup
signature.description: Receives the state's parameters; may return an object of provider-state values.

signature.name: teardown
signature.description: Optional. Receives the state's parameters.

primitives.semantics: Declares a loopback 'http' hook (lifecycle-hooks spec §8.4, ADR 0055 decision 2). The n-th state handler declared on a verifier, counting from 1, is named 'state-<n>'. At 'verify', it is a 'state-setup' entry { name, when: { state }, run: { kind: 'http', url, headers: { authorization } } } and, when it has a teardown, a 'state-teardown' entry with the same name, 'when' and 'run' shape. The url is 'http://127.0.0.1:<port>/<point>/<name>' on the endpoint the SDK serves for the run; the header is 'Bearer ' and the run's token, at least 128 random bits written as hex, the same in every entry the SDK writes. No other member is written: the engine's defaults apply (policy, deadline, retries). When the engine POSTs a hook context to the entry's url with that header, the SDK calls 'setup' (at 'state-setup') or 'teardown' (at 'state-teardown') with the context's 'state.params', or an empty object when it has none, and answers 200 with an invoke result: a returned object is { outcome: 'ok', values: <the object> }; nothing returned is { outcome: 'ok' }; a thrown failure is { outcome: 'failed', error: { code: 'handler-failed', message: <the failure's message> } }; the handler saying it cannot reach the state, in the way the style guide records, is { outcome: 'unsupported', error: { code: 'state-unsupported', message: <its reason> } }. A request without the run's token is answered 401 with an empty body and calls nothing; a path that names no handler is answered 404. The SDK retries nothing and orders nothing: the engine decides when each runs (lifecycle-hooks spec §3.2, §3.7).

errors.surfaced-as: thrown from 'verify' when the engine cannot run 'http' hooks, as any engine error; the run never starts

facade.reason: one handler per state name with the same setup and teardown functions and the same returned values; the default supplied is that a handler runs over a loopback socket, where today's runs in process — nothing it can observe differs but the time a call takes.

facade.from: pact-jvm @State(value, action) methods taking the state's parameters and returning a Map of values
facade.reason: @State methods on the test class, its superclasses and interfaces, declared as state handlers by the JUnit extension; a state with no method has no hook and its exchange runs without setup, where pact-jvm fails it (ADR 0056 decision 3).

primitives.summary: Changes each request before it is sent to the provider — a token, a signature — in the test's own code.

signature.name: filter
signature.description: Receives the request and returns it, changed.

signature.name: options
signature.description: Optional { changes }: the request slots the filter changes, by slot name. Default: [ 'headers' ].

primitives.semantics: Declares a loopback 'http' hook at 'before-request' (lifecycle-hooks spec §3.3, ADR 0055 decision 2). The n-th request filter declared on a verifier, counting from 1, is named 'request-filter-<n>', and its entry is { name, changes, run }, 'run' as a state handler's is and 'changes' the declared slots, each written 'parts.request.<slot>', in the order given. When the engine POSTs a hook context, the filter receives the request: an object with a member per slot of the context's 'parts.request', each that slot's 'content'. It returns the request in the same form. The SDK answers 200 with { outcome: 'ok', changes: { 'parts.request.<slot>': { content: <the returned request's slot> } } } for each declared slot the returned request has, in the declared order, and compares nothing: what changed is not the SDK's to decide. A filter that returns nothing is { outcome: 'ok' }; a thrown failure is { outcome: 'failed', error: { code: 'handler-failed', message } }. A request without the run's token is answered 401 and calls nothing.

errors.surfaced-as: thrown from 'verify' when the engine refuses a declared slot that is not a context path, as any engine error; the run never starts

facade.from: pact-js requestFilter (an Express middleware (req, res, next))
facade.reason: a function from the request to the request; the default supplied is that it changes headers only unless it declares other slots, because an entry must declare what it may change before the run (lifecycle-hooks spec §4.3).
a request filter declared on the Verifier the JUnit extension runs; it receives the request's slots, not the HTTP client's request object (ADR 0056 decision 3).

primitives.summary: Produces a message the provider would send, in the test's own code, for the engine to compare with the one a pact expects.

signature.name: description
signature.description: The message interaction's description, exactly as the pact or contract records it.

signature.name: produce
signature.description: Receives the request for the message and returns the message: a body, and optionally a content type and metadata.

primitives.semantics: Declares a loopback 'http' hook at 'produce-message' (lifecycle-hooks spec §3.4, ADR 0056 decision 1). The n-th message producer declared on a verifier, counting from 1, is named 'message-<n>', and its entry is { name, when: { interaction: <description> }, changes: [ 'parts' ], run }, 'run' as a state handler's is. When the engine POSTs a hook context, the producer receives the context's 'interaction.pact-message.request' (what today's verifier POSTs to ask for the message: its description, its provider states and a synchronous message's request), or an empty object when the context has none. It returns a message: a body, which is bytes, a string or any other value, and optionally a content type and an object of metadata. The SDK answers 200 with { outcome: 'ok', changes: { parts: { message: { metadata: { content: <object> }, body: { content: <base64>, encoded: 'base64' } } } } }. The body's octets are the bytes as given, a string's UTF-8 encoding, or any other value's JSON text in UTF-8; 'body' also has 'content-type', the content type, when one was given, and is otherwise unlabelled: the engine reads an unlabelled message's type from its metadata's 'contentType', else from its octets (ADR 0049), and the SDK detects nothing. The metadata object is { contentType: <the content type> } when one was given, else empty, with each member of the returned metadata written over it. A thrown failure is { outcome: 'failed', error: { code: 'handler-failed', message } }. A request without the run's token is answered 401 and calls nothing. The SDK writes no producer of its own: a message no producer answers is the engine's 'message-not-produced' (ADR 0046).

errors.surfaced-as: not thrown: a message no producer answered is a failed result naming 'hook/produce-message' with reason 'message-not-produced', which fails 'verify' as any failed result does

primitives.summary: Runs the verification, and fails when the run failed.
primitives.semantics: In order (ADR 0055 decisions 1 and 3). Read every path in 'pacts' as UTF-8 JSON, before anything else; a file that cannot be read or parsed fails 'verify' with no engine started. Start the engine and send 'engine/hello' offering protocol version 1. When 'config' is given, send 'config/load' with its path, resolved against the working directory when it has no root (the rule 'janus' states for a component reference) and with no '.' or '..' segment left in it; the answer's 'hooks' and 'components' are the configuration. Start the loopback endpoint, when any handler is declared. Send one 'verification/verify': 'source' is { kind: 'inline', contracts: <the documents as read, in the order given> }, or the 'broker' or 'urls' option with its 'kind' added, members as given; 'target' is { transports: [ { transport: 'http', options: { 'base-url': <the provider URL>, and each member of the 'transport' option beside it, as given } } ] }, with 'components' the configuration's then the option's, each as 'janus' passes one, present when either has any, and 'hooks' { version, hooks } present when a configuration was loaded or a handler declared — 'version' the configuration's or 1, and at each point the configuration's entries, then the handlers' in declaration order (state handlers and request filters, ADR 0055; message producers, ADR 0056); 'options' the run's options as given, with 'report': {} added when they have no 'report' member (ADR 0059): a caller that gives 'report' itself is sent what it gave. Then send 'events/poll' for the returned stream until an event carrying 'last: true' arrives, collecting the payload of every 'verification/interaction-result' as the run's results, in order, and of every 'verification/warning' as its warnings, in order (ADR 0058). Each 'verification/report' event's 'text' is written to the process's standard output as it arrives, followed by a line break, and when the run has ended, one empty line more if any was written, to set the report apart from what the test runner prints next; nothing else is written: that is the run's report, laid out by the engine, which says the warnings too, so a test shows what the run did as pact-js's does (ADR 0059). The terminal event's payload is the summary. Then stop the endpoint and end the engine; they are stopped and ended however 'verify' ends, the engine's errors and thrown failures included. The result is { status: <the summary's status>, summary, results, warnings }. A status 'failed' fails 'verify', carrying that result, and naming each result whose status is 'failed' and which is not 'pending'. 'verified' and 'filtered' return the result: a filtered run is not a failure, and its status says 'filtered', never 'verified' (ADR 0041). A pending result's failure fails nothing: the summary's status already says what the run decided. Any operation answered with an error fails 'verify' with that error, and nothing more is sent but the engine's end.
